sources.headline: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
sources.text: Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed a "serious" response to the deadly attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement."The events of recent weeks are serious. Our response must be equally serious," Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh.On Sunday, a Pakistani man was killed in an attack on a terminal at the capital's King Khalid International Airport, Saudi authorities said. It came a day after a Houthi missile hit another terminal, killing 13 people and forcing its closure.The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for "brutal Saudi aggression" against areas they control in western Yemen.The Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six other people were injured in a Saudi air strike on a home in the capital, Sanaa, on Sunday.A Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces battling the Houthis on Yemen's Red Sea coast and other areas.Explosions were heard again in Riyadh on Monday night, with the Saudi-led military coalition saying a ballistic missile had been intercepted and destroyed.A Houthi spokesperson said the group had again targeted the airport.The WPC Energy Congress opened on Sunday at a convention centre about 10km (6 miles) from Riyadh's airport, which has been attacked four times over the past week.Last Thursday, three Saudis, including a pilot for the national airline Saudia, were killed in two strikes on an airport facility and an aircraft on the ground.Another four Saudis, as well as two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian, one Sudanese and one Indian, were killed in Saturday's missile strike on Terminal 3.On Sunday, a Pakistani resident was killed when a projectile hit Terminal 4, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).King Fahd International Airport in the north-eastern city of Dammam was also attacked on Sunday evening, it said, but no casualties were reported.Later, the Saudi-led coalition said its forces had intercepted a drone in Eastern Province and a missile launched by the Houthis towards the south-western city of Khamis Mushait.In his inaugural address to the WPC Energy Congress on Monday, Prince Abdul Aziz thanked industry executives and policymakers for attending despite the attacks."You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart," he said.But he also acknowledged that "energy security cannot be taken for granted" and that recent developments had "tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience".Prince Abdul Aziz promised that his country would overcome those challenges."We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people," he said. "We shall prove it to the world that whatever we are going through we will overcome it."There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.On Sunday evening, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a video statement that its forces had launched missiles and drones at Riyadh and Dammam's airports, as well as two oil and gas facilities in Eastern Province, in response to 124 Saudi air strikes in Yemen over the previous 24 hours.Sarea also reiterated a warning to airlines and passengers against using Saudi airports and airspace, except for journeys to and from the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina.The Houthis' forces, he vowed, would "continue their escalating operations deep inside Saudi, imposing the equation of 'a blockade for a blockade' and 'an escalation for an escalation' and targeting Saudi enemy reinforcements until the aggression ceases and the siege on our dear people is lifted".Saturday's attack on Riyadh airport drew widespread international condemnation.UN Secretary General António Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" and warned that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure were a violation of international law.President Donald Trump said he would "make a decision" about the US joining Saudi Arabia's strikes on the Houthis. The US military is reportedly already providing intelligence and targeting support to the Saudi-led coalition.Iran, which has repeatedly denied allegations that it provides weapons and training to the Houthis, said it was "deeply concerned" by the escalation and called for "dialogue and engagement" to resolve the situation.Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing.Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea.They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

sources.headline: Saudi Arabia further suspends flights after latest deadly Houthi attack on airport
sources.text: Saudi Arabia has been forced to suspend all flights to and from its main international airport in Riyadh until next Saturday after a further round of Houthi missile attacks caused more damage and left one person dead. Some airlines, including Gulf Air and Bahrain Air, had already said they were cancelling flights until next Saturday. More missiles were fired at Saudi Arabian cities by the Houthis on Monday, Saudi Arabian’s military spokesperson said.The Gulf nation announced it was suspending flights from Riyadh, its second busiest airport, after Houthi missiles killed 13 people on Saturday and left more than 300 injured. Saudi state TV broadcast CCTV footage that showed passengers deluged in smoke and falling masonry as they queued at the airport terminal to board a plane just as the Houthi missile struck.Before and after the strike as people queue up for flights at King Khalid international airport on Saturday. Photograph: Saudi Ministry of Media/ReutersThe country has pressed ahead with the 25th WPC Energy Conference in Riyadh, hoping to project an image of normality. But some senior oil executives did not attend or appeared virtually.The Saudi energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman, told the conference that “fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon”, emphasising the resilience of the kingdom’s energy system and the determination of its people to confront crises. Amin Nasser, the president and chief executive of Aramco, said Saudi Arabia had invested deeply in protecting its supplies, but “no nation, even one as capable and confident as ours, can safeguard them alone.”He added: “Markets can diversify suppliers. They cannot diversify geography […] when energy infrastructure in this region is targeted, the consequences reach economies everywhere.”An urgent review is under way as to how Houthi missiles are repeatedly penetrating badly stretched Saudi air defences. Schoolchildren and some office workers were advised to work from home. The Houthis have also targeted the city of Khamis Mushait, and the King Fahd international airport in Dammam.Interceptor missiles are needed to protect government buildings, oil facilities and infrastructure hubs across a wide geographic area. The Houthis have vowed to attack Saudi airports across the country.Houthi attacks since last month have targeted fuel tanks at Riyadh airport and its affiliated warehouses, destroying a parked Airbus A320 passenger plane and damaging at least five other aircraft.The crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, has not been seen in public since Tuesday last week, reflecting the pressure he is under to find a way out from a war that has intermittently dogged his leadership since 2014. Saudi Arabia badly needs stability to continue the slow diversification of its economy from oil dependence, but has not found a way to restore it in Yemen.Inside Yemen, fighting continued in and around Taiz, the third city, and the most populous governorate, with Saudi planes mounting eight separate strikes on any assembly of Houthi forces. As many as 60 fighters died on Sunday from both sides.The governor of Taiz, Nabil Shamsan, on Sunday issued an urgent call to lift the Houthi siege and warned a shortage of medicines meant the city would soon run out of emergency surgical and intensive care services.Overall the Houthis claimed the Saudis had mounted 124 raids on Sunday. The Saudis are seeking to locate Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, with rumours of his assassination repeatedly circulating, but Saudi Arabia does not seem to have contemporary intelligence on his precise whereabouts either in the capital Sana’a or in its stronghold of Saada.A billboard displays an image of the Houthi leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, in Sana’a, Yemen on Sunday. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAOn the diplomatic front, Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, spoke to the Saudi foreign minister, Faisal bin Farhan, on Sunday to see if there was a way in which Iran could act as a mediator between the Saudis and the Houthis, a group that Iran has trained and armed. Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthi Political Bureau claimed Saudi Arabia accepted the mediation offered by Iran and proposed first a one-month truce, and then a two week truce, but the Houthis had rejected both offers.He said “the battle this time is not like its predecessors; the arena is no longer the same arena, and the cards have changed. Therefore, a comprehensive settlement must be put in place between Riyadh and Sana’a, the Houthi capital because every day that passes in this battle will expand its scope and deepen its losses, and the settlement that is possible today may become difficult or impossible tomorrow”.A meeting of the UN security council in New York on Tuesday is expected to debate a resolution calling the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation.The exiled leader of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), Aidarous al-Zubaidi, called for southern forces to fight on all fronts, and not just to defend the borders of the former South Yemen, in a move that is likely to be welcomed by Saudi Arabia as it supports the week-old call by the UN-recognised government to drive the Houthis out of the whole of Yemen, rather than just from the southern governorates.The STC has a vision of an independent South Yemen that would recreate the separate state that existed between 1967 and 1990. The reunification of Yemen at the end of the cold war proved fragile and many southerners nurse longstanding grievances about the distribution of resources in the unified state.The STC’s authority has been challenged by Abd al-Rahman al-Mahrami, the Salafist leader who commands the powerful Southern Giants Brigades.Despite Araghchi’s efforts to reach out to the Saudis, Mohsen Rezaei, the more hardline secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, claimed Iran was hitting five or six small vessels in the strait of Hormuz every night, explaining the vessels were being used by the Emirati military to move oil through the strait to larger tankers, thus breaching the blockade that Iran is seeking to maintain to push up oil prices and weaken Donald Trump.Esmail Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, said Trump’s treatment of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including his call for the Ukrainian president to stand aside showed the risks in dealing with Trump. He said: “Being an enemy of America can be dangerous, but being a friend of America is deadly. You can see for yourself what America’s friendship and enmity with its allies is like.”

sources.text: The Saudi authorities said they were fending off drone and missile attacks after a weekend of confrontation with the Houthi militia in Yemen, whose patrons Iran offered to mediate.

sources.headline: Fact check: Viral videos falsely linked to Riyadh airport attacks
sources.text:
Yemen's Houthi rebels have claimed responsibility for a series of attacks on Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International Airport in recent days. At least 16 people have been killed since last Thursday, according to Saudi authorities.
As news of the attacks spreads, social media users have been sharing videos that they claim show the strikes. While some authentic footage of the attacks and their aftermath has circulated online, DW Fact check found that several viral videos are not genuine and show signs of being AI-generated.
This AI-generated video has been circulating since March and contains several inconsistenciesImage: X
Claim: This post with 1.7 million views on X, claims it shows the moment of an attack on the airport.
DW Fact check: Fake
The video has been online since March 2026 and could not show the most recent attacks on the airport.
Hectic camera movements and blurry footage help conceal glitches that often point to AI-generated content. However, our frame-by-frame analysis identified several inconsistencies. That suggests the video was AI-generated.
In the video, people run toward an exit as an explosion occurs outside. Despite the apparent danger, they continue moving toward the blast, seemingly through a glass door. This reaction is implausible.
Around 10 seconds into the video, an image of a hand holding a smartphone appears on the side of a man's head.
At 12 seconds, one man first appears not to have a hand, then miraculously has one.
A side-by-side comparison shows a hand appear out of nowhereImage: X
Meta's AI identification tool finds AI signatures in the video and concludes it was created using generative AI.
Many shared the video as authentic, including the Times of Israel– its post had more than 256,000 views at the time of writing.
The video has appeared in many languages, including Arabic, English, Russian, Spanish, Turkish, Nepali, and it has been shared on YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, Facebookand other platforms.
AI generates video from real photograph
Claim: In this post on X with 2.9 million views, a user claims it shows "new video footage of the moment King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh was targeted." AI can generate videos from still photographsImage: X
DW Fact check: Fake
The video is AI-generated and contains several inconsistencies when compared with the real airport. Using a reverse image search, we found the photograph used to generate the fake video.
The original image was uploaded to stock photo database Shutterstockin 2016. Although it was taken from a slightly different angle it shows many visual cues that overlap with the video, including the white triangular geometric patterns of the airport building roof, the dome to the left, the luggage transport vehicles and the open and closed doors of the plane.
Other elements are missing. In the video, the light pole to the left of the aircraft appears without any lamps attached. The video is grainy and contains some visual glitches where parts of the image suddenly become blurry.
When the supposed missile strikes the plane, a nearby vehicle significantly changes its shape as it is thrown into the air. Another inconsistency is that, despite the missile's massive explosion and a resulting fireball, nearby objects do not cast corresponding shadows.
The account that shared the video has repeatedly posted AI-generated content in the past.
Whereas the October 8 attack at King Khalid International Airport did reportedly badly damage a plane, this video does not show the moment of attack.
Video predates attack and shows people move through objects
Claim: This TikTok postwith more than 301,000 views claims that the footage was recorded "just now from the heart of Riyadh Airport."
AI-generated videos often contain impossible scenarios, like people walking through objectsImage: Tik Tok
DW Fact check: Fake
This video had already circulated online in March 2026, months before the attack. We found the video was shared in Greek, Albanian, Turkish and Russian.
The footage contains several visual anomalies. Parts of the image appear blurry, and some people seem to merge into one another. In addition, a row of red lights in the terminal switches on one second before the supposed explosion becomes visible through the window.
The clearest indication that the video is AI-generated is the way people move through the queue barriers. At the beginning of the video, several people appear to walk directly through them. After the supposed explosion, some individuals run straight through barriers that appear to end mid-air and are connected on only one side.
Video contains Google AI watermarks
Claim: This TikTok post, which has garnered more than 500,000 views, reports on the attacks on the airports in Riyadh and Abha and includes a compilation of videos. We examined the first video.
Since August 2026, the EU's AI Act requires AI-generated content to carry machine-readable markingsImage: Tik Tok
DW Fact check: Fake
Analysis using Google Gemini detected that the video was generated, at least in part, with Google AI tools. The clip contains a SynthID watermark in both the images and the audio.
The same video also circulated on Facebook, where it has received more than 157,000 views. On Facebook it has been posted by an account that only shares AI-generated videos, and it is clearly labeled as "AI-content."
All four videos examined by DW Fact check are very short. Two are between six and ten seconds long, while the other two last 13 and 15 seconds, respectively. Such brief videos are easier to create with AI and often contain very little visual information, making it difficult for viewers to verify their authenticity.
Daniel Ebertz contributed to this research.
Edited by: Chiponda Chimbelu

Saudi Arabia faces more drone, missile attacks after Houthi’s fatal airport strikes

Published: 8:23pm, 12 Oct 2026Updated: 8:23pm, 12 Oct 2026

Saudi Arabia said it was dealing with new drone and cruise missile attacks on Monday, posing fresh security threats to the kingdom following the weekend’s deadly strikes on Riyadh airport.

“We have detected and are monitoring a threat involving drones and cruise missiles against the kingdom and the threat is being dealt with,” the state-run Saudi Press Agency reported.

It cited Defence Ministry spokesman Turki al-Maliki on behalf of a Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis.

The coalition said earlier it had intercepted missiles and drones aimed at the kingdom overnight, including areas that are home to some of Saudi Arabia’s key oil and gas facilities.

Saudi authorities on Monday extended a suspension of operations at the King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, where two separate attacks over the weekend killed at least 14 people and wounded more than 300, many critically.

King Fahd International Airport in Dammam was targeted separately.

Meanwhile, air strikes on two districts in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa killed one person and wounded 12 others, according to the Houthis.

Their media centre blamed Saudi Arabia for the strikes.

01:01
Houthi attack on Saudi airport kills 12, injures hundreds

The weekend’s events mark the deadliest strikes for Saudi Arabia since the Iran war began and come a week after Saudi-led forces in Yemen launched a campaign to retake areas held by Houthi militia, including the Bab el-Mandeb strait and “eliminate” the group.

As the violence stretched into Monday, the coalition vowed a “decisive” response.

There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix. We come out of the ashes all the time and every time
Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman

Against that backdrop, Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, one of the most senior Saudi officials to speak publicly in the wake of the strikes, sought to project resilience, telling oil industry executives that the kingdom remained committed to providing energy security.

“There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix. We come out of the ashes all the time and every time,” Prince Abdulaziz said at an energy event on Sunday.

At the World Petroleum Congress (WPC) on Monday, he called for a serious response to events of recent weeks, while noting the country should remain focused on economic diversification and investment.

Guests attend the 25th World Petroleum Council in Riyadh on Monday. Photo: AFP

The WPC gathering has been disrupted by the hostilities, with some executives who had been scheduled to attend, including the chief executives of BP Plc and Shell Plc, withdrawing.

Riyadh has been in conflict with Houthi militants ever since they took control over the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, in 2014 and forced the internationally recognised government backed by Saudi Arabia to resign the following year.

US President Donald Trump said over the weekend he was considering joining in the fight against the Iran-backed militant group.

“The attack last night is very emblematic. A very advanced, sophisticated ballistic missile, very accurate, targeting a commercial airport and now a number of civilian casualties,” former White House Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk told Bloomberg Television.

“It’s an act of terrorism. I think there has to be a response.”

A combination picture shows surveillance footage of people right before and at the moment of an attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Saturday. Photo: Handout via Reuters

A senior United Arab Emirates official, meanwhile, urged a revival of regional security arrangements.

“It has become evident that we are all targets and that our security is indivisible,” Anwar Gargash, senior adviser to the UAE president, said on X.

Brent crude extended gains to above US$105 a barrel on Monday following the weekend strikes.

Traders weighed resilient Middle East flows against rising regional tensions and a US claim that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a so-called energy ceasefire.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea delivers a televised statement in Sana’a, Yemen, on Sunday. Photo: EPA

The Saudi civil aviation authority said one person died and 11 were injured after an unknown projectile hit the main airport in Riyadh on Sunday.

That followed a strike on King Khalid airport on Saturday.

The attacks brought travel at the Riyadh airport to a near-standstill. They also forced the capital’s financial hub to shift to remote work and schools to do remote learning.

The FAA on Sunday issued a warning to all US airlines to exercise caution flying to or over parts of Saudi Arabia “at all altitudes”.

Authorities have indicated the 25th World Petroleum Congress and associated events, scheduled to run until Wednesday, will continue.

Riyadh is also scheduled to host the Future Investment Initiative (FII), its flagship investor gathering, later this month.

The two events draw industry heavyweights and thousands of delegates.

“Comprehensive security measures will be in place at Riyadh’s airports, our conference venues and official hotels, with coordinated arrangements for participants’ transportation and movements,” the FII’s Chief Executive Officer, Maha Al Saud, said in a statement.

Additional reporting by Associated Press

sources.headline: Riyadh airport stays closed as Saudis probe failures in deadly attack
sources.text: Yemen's Houthis say they have launched another attack on Riyadh airport and an air base in Saudi Arabia's Khamis Mushait as fighting between the two sides continues. Saudi Arabia earlier issued an alert for a potential "hostile threat" in Riyadh, according to a message seen by Reuters.A Saudi-led coalition later said it had destroyed the ballistic missile fired by the Iran-aligned group.An alert was later issued over a potential danger in Khamis Mushait which officials have since said has passed.The latest strikes came after Saudi officials launched an investigation into how its air defences failed to intercept the barrage of missiles and drones that struck King Khalid International Airport, killing 14 people and injuring about 320 on the weekend.The Houthis have been attacking Saudi airports and oil facilities since last week as part of a rapidly escalating conflict that has spilled over from the war between the United States and Iran.Authorities have extended the closure of the airport until October 17 and airlines have scrapped flights.UAE airline Etihad said it would not resume flights until next week at the earliest.Thick black smoke and flames rise from a fire at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. (AP)The Saudi civil aviation authority said work was underway to "allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport's facilities".Air traffic tracker Flightradar24 showed planes avoiding the city on Monday, though jets were crossing Saudi airspace and landing at the country's biggest airport in Jeddah on the country's west coast. Officials, who spoke to the Associated Press on condition of anonymity, said an initial probe showed the Houthis first fired multiple drones to pave the way for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles to reach King Khalid International Airport.One of the officials said the investigation also aimed to find out why air defence systems did not provide earlier warning of the attack in which the missiles and drones flew more than 1,000 kilometres to reach Riyadh."The events of recent weeks are serious," Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the World Petroleum Energy Congress in Riyadh."Our response must be equally serious."The Saudi government-run Center for International Communication, which oversees foreign media, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Strikes have continued between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, with the rebel group saying one person had been killed and 12 injured in a new Saudi attack on the Yemeni capital Sanaa.Saudi officials want US more involvedDonald Trump spoke with reporters on Saturday. (AP: Alex Brandon)The Saudis are looking to the US to become more directly involved in their fight against the Houthis.The US has provided intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for a Saudi-led offensive — but so far has held off on directly carrying out strikes against the Houthis.US President Donald Trump on Saturday told reporters that he was looking at the possibility of carrying out US attacks against the Houthis.Speaking at a conference in Abu Dhabi focused on the postwar future of the Middle East, former US secretary of state Mike Pompeo said the Houthi strike was a troubling development that showed the US had not yet achieved its objectives for the war against Iran."What it does demonstrate is that we've not yet achieved deterrence. We collectively have not yet achieved deterrence," said Mr Pompeo, who served as secretary of state and CIA director during Mr Trump's first term."You have to crush the Iranian regime, period, full stop. There's no solution short of that."A US intervention could prompt the Houthis to try to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen, restricting the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf.UAE diplomat suggests Gulf allies respond to Houthis jointlySeparately, an Emirati diplomat on Monday called for "joint Gulf action" to defend Gulf countries against attacks by Iran and its allies.Anwar Gargash — a diplomatic adviser to the rulers of the United Arab Emirates — said Iran and its allies wrongly assessed that Gulf Arabs were "the weakest link" in the US war against Iran, during which Tehran and its allies repeatedly attacked Arab countries on the other side of the Gulf.Anwar Gargash is the Emirati minister of state for foreign affairs. (AP: Ebrahim Noroozi)"It has become clear that we are all targeted, and that our security is indivisible," he wrote on social media, adding that attacks on Saudi Arabia "undermine the security of the UAE and all Gulf states".AP/Reuters

sources.headline: Saudi airport stays shut as Houthi attacks kill 20 people in a week
sources.text:
18m ago
Delta delays planned flights from Atlanta to Riyadh amid attacks on airports
Delta Air Lines said Monday it is delaying plans for nonstop flights from Atlanta to Riyadh amid escalating attacks between Yemen's Houthi militants and Saudi Arabia."The safety and security of our customers and employees always come first and continue to guide our operational decisions," the company said in a statement. "We remain in close contact with relevant government and aviation partners, including Saudia and Riyadh Air, as we monitor the situation."Delta announced last year its plans to operate nonstop flights to Riyadh three times a week on its Airbus A350-900 aircraft in October 2026. It said at the time that the new destination would help strengthen business and travel ties between the United States and Saudi Arabia.The company said Monday the launch of Atlanta-Riyadh flights will take place in March 2027.Read more here.
41m ago
Iran's foreign ministry says U.K.'s accusations are unfounded
Iran's Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday denied the U.K.'s allegations that Tehran was involved in last month's security incident at a British base used by American bombers.In a statement posted to social media, the foreign ministry condemned what it said were "unfounded accusations by the United Kingdom against Iran."U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier Monday the security incident at RAF Fairford — which led to the arrests of seven men who were later released on bail — was "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran" and "almost certainly" by the regime's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. In its response, Tehran said by using terms like "highly likely" and "almost" certain, the U.K. is "hiding behind vague language without presenting concrete evidence or proof."
4:02 PM
NATO countries issue joint statement on Iran and RAF Fairford security incident
Foreign ministers of NATO member countries on Monday issued a joint statement condemning "Iran's use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners."The statement said the countries recognize the U.K.'s assertion that last month's security incident at RAF Fairford, a U.S.-run air base in Britain, was likely coordinated by Iran."Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable," the joint statement said. " Anyone who conducts hostile activities on behalf of Iran, or any other state, should know that we will take action to identify, investigate, disrupt, and prosecute these acts."In a separate statement, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said he welcomes the statement issued by allies and partners, echoing their denouncement of "Iran's involvement in violence and threats on Allied territory.""NATO will continue to do its part to safeguard the security of our one billion people across the Alliance," Rutte said.
3:39 PM
Houthis confirm they targeted Riyadh's airport again with ballistic missile
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis claimed an attack targeting Riyadh's international airport on Monday, after a Saudi-led coalition said it had shot down a missile over the capital."Our armed forces were able to target (King) Khalid International Airport in the Saudi enemy's capital Riyadh this evening with a ballistic missile and the hit was precise," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said. He said the group also targeted the Khamis Mushait base in the kingdom's south with a drone.Saree also warned against "the consequences of operating flights toward Saudi airports, as they are not safe, with the exception of the airports and airspace of the sacred areas in Mecca al-Mukarramah and Medina al-Munawwarah."It's unclear whether there were any injuries.CBS/AFP
2:40 PM
Multiple blasts heard in Riyadh, as residents warned of aerial threat
Several powerful explosions rattled the Saudi capital Riyadh on Monday night, just moments after a text message sent to residents' mobile phones warned of an aerial threat."The area is under a hostile aerial threat. Please remain calm, stay indoors or in a safe place away from windows and doors," read the message.Around the same time, the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said its forces intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-backed group at the capital."Interception and destruction of a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh," Major General Turki al-Malki, a spokesperson for the coalition, wrote in a post on X.
2:05 PM
U.K. foreign minister announces sanctions against 2 Iranian nationals
U.K. Foreign Minister Ed Miliband announced sanctions against two Iranian nationals on Monday, "for their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas," he said in a statement."We will not tolerate threats on British soil," said Miliband, who earlier had released a joint statement alongside his counterparts in the U.S., Australia, Canada and 23 other countries, which condemned hostile activities by Iran on foreign soil.Their statements followed a security incident at the RAF Fairford air base in southern England, which U.K. government leaders and others have attributed to Iran. Iran denied its involvement Monday in comments released by state media.
1:35 PM
Americans detained for photographing attacks in Saudi Arabia, U.S. embassy says
The U.S. embassy in Riyadh said on Monday that American citizens had been detained for filming recent events in Saudi Arabia, which has suffered a string of deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis.The embassy said "American citizens have been detained for taking photos of recent events," without specifying how many were arrested or whether they had been released. It noted that Saudi authorities have warned that "filming, publishing, or sharing information related to counter missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability."Several foreign residents in Riyadh have told AFP that acquaintances were detained for filming recent events and sharing the footage on social media.
1:24 PM
Iran denies involvement in U.K. air base incident, state media reports
Iran on Monday denied any involvement in a security incident at England's RAF Fairford air base, which the U.S. previously used to deploy long-range bombers during the war. "The Iranian ambassador in London, Ali Moussavi, has again categorically rejected the accusations concerning Tehran's role in the incident at the Fairford military base," the Iranian state news agency IRNA reported, adding that he "called on the British government to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any."That statement followed earlier remarks from British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who said the incident was "almost certainly directed" by Iran's Revolutionary Guard.CBS/AFP
12:43 PM
Iran claims to have struck 3 supertankers in the Strait of Hormuz in the last 2 days
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Monday to have struck three supertankers in the Strait of Hormuz over the last two days.The IRGC Navy said in its most recent attack on a ship, Monday, "a third non-compliant super-tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire."It said the tanker had switched off the system that broadcasts a vessel's location in an effort to evade Iranian restrictions on navigating the strait without permission and "disregarded warnings from the IRGC Navy."The statement warned that "any cooperation by commercial vessels and oil tankers with the invading, plundering American terrorist and smuggling army in the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf region will be met with a decisive response from us."President Trump and his senior aides have insisted for weeks that a southern route through the strait, skirting close to Oman's coast, is safe and available, and the U.S. military has escorted an increasing number of ships along that route in recent weeks. Iran rejects that route and demands that all vessels use a northern passage close to its own coastline, seeking permission from its military.The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center, which monitors incidents in the region, had not reported any attacks on vessels Monday, but it noted at least two projectiles hitting vessels Sunday.

U.S., U.K., Australia, Canada and others condemn Iranian attacks, including "hybrid activities," after air base incident
The foreign ministers of the U.S., the U.K., Australia, Canada and 23 other countries, many in Europe, have released a joint statement condemning hostile activities by Iran on foreign soil.The statement came on the heels of British Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying a recent security incident at England's RAF Fairford air base, which was until recently home to U.S. long-range bombers, was "almost certainly

sources.headline: Houthi official warns of ‘swift, painful response’ if US enters Yemen war
sources.text: SANAA - A Houthi official on Oct 12 warned the US it would receive a “painful response” if it entered the war in Yemen, where Saudi Arabia has reportedly requested Washington’s help in dealing with the group as it weathers repeated attacks.Yemen’s civil war – in which a Saudi-led military coalition supports the government against the Iran-backed Houthis – reignited in July, months into the wider regional conflict that has roiled energy markets and plunged the Middle East into crisis.The Houthis quickly began targeting Saudi oil facilities, tankers and transport hubs, including with a string of lethal strikes on Riyadh’s airport, rocking the world’s top oil exporter.Blasts resounded over the capital again on the night of Oct 12, with the Saudi coalition saying it had intercepted a Houthi missile and the group saying it had, again, targeted the airport.Following an attack on Oct 10 at the facility that killed 13 people, US President Donald Trump said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the group, after having reportedly rebuffed previous requests for help from the kingdom.“If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond, rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region,” Houthi political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti told AFP in an interview.He also warned “all employees and workers at Saudi oil facilities and airports to stay away from these sites, as they have become legitimate targets”.The Oct 10 strike on King Khalid International Airport was the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in more than a decade, and also left hundreds wounded.Trump said the attack was “not acceptable” and that he would be speaking to the kingdom’s de facto leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, telling reporters the US was “going to look at” the possibility of joining Saudi strikes.Operations remained suspended at the sprawling airport on Riyadh’s outskirts on Oct 12.‘Serious’ responseBukhaiti said the purpose of the campaign against Saudi targets was to send a message to the crown prince “that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position”.Saudi energy minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told a conference in Riyadh on Oct 12 that the recent events had “tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience”.“The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious.”CCTV footage of Oct 10’s attack released by Saudi authorities showed Muslim pilgrims in religious attire waiting in departure lounges before a sudden blast tore through the building and brought down flaming debris.The atmosphere in Riyadh remained tense on Oct 12, as state broadcaster Al Ekhbariya said the military coalition was responding to drone and missile threats.In the evening, mobile phones received a loud government alert warning of a “hostile aerial threat” before the announcement of the interception.It was the first use of the phone alert system in Riyadh in weeks, with no official reason given for the lack of messaging during the attacks targeting the capital in recent days.The Houthis said they had also targeted the Khamis Mushait base in the kingdom’s south with a drone.Flights suspendedThe US embassy in Saudi Arabia said US government employees must obtain its authorisation before using any airport in the kingdom, and urged US citizens to “take extreme caution” if they chose to do so.The mission also said “American citizens have been detained for taking photos of recent events” in Saudi Arabia.The UAE’s national carrier Etihad Airways announced on Oct 12 that it was cancelling all flights to and from Riyadh until next week, and also suspended flights to Dammam and Jeddah.Bahrain’s national carrier Gulf Air said it too was cancelling all Riyadh flights until Oct 17.US operator Delta announced it would delay the launch of direct flights from Atlanta to Riyadh, scheduled for Oct 23.Despite vast spending on military hardware, the Houthi attacks on oil, military and transport facilities across the large, mostly desert country are stretching Saudi defences.Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University, said that despite some success, “Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves”.Riyadh leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen’s government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.Juneau said the Houthis now “want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them”.The long-running Yemeni civil war has created a deeply entrenched humanitarian crisis in the impoverished country.UN rights chief Volker Turk said he was “appalled by the repeated attacks” on Saudi Arabia, but urged both sides to back down, adding “continued fighting will only unleash further misery with no end in sight”. AFP

sources.headline: Saudi health minister visits survivors of deadly Riyadh airport attack
Riyadh airport strikes claimed by Yemen's Houthi day after deadliest attack in Saudi soil in ten years
sources.text:
Yemen’s Houthis have continued their strikes on Riyadh’s international airport after a missile attack on Saturday killed 13 people and injured more than 300.
A projectile struck a passenger terminal at King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, causing a fire. Saudi aviation authorities said a Pakistani national was killed and 11 people were injured in the latest attack.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks, which have escalated following renewed fighting in the war in Yemen and raised the prospect of greater US military involvement.
The death toll from Saturday’s attack rose to 13 on Sunday after an Indian national died of his injuries, according to India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia.
Saudi aviation authorities had initially reported 12 deaths and 309 injuries, some critical. Those killed included four Saudi citizens and eight foreign nationals, including a US citizen.
The Saudi-led coalition blamed the Iran-backed Houthis for Saturday’s attack, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, and vowed a decisive response.
The Houthis renewed their warning on Sunday to airlines, airport workers and travellers against using Saudi airports, saying the facilities remained vulnerable to attack.
Trump weighs US involvement
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that Washington might join Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
Asked whether the US would take part, Trump told reporters, “We may. We’re going to look at it.” He did not announce a decision to join the strikes.
He later said Saudi Arabia could defend itself against the Houthis and described the airport attack as “terrible”.
In a separate incident, the coalition said a projectile fell near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Saturday.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called Saturday’s Riyadh attack a “dangerous escalation” and expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia.
“These attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence,” she said, warning of the threat to international transport and energy infrastructure.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres also condemned the attack.
“Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately,” he said in a statement issued on Saturday.
Qatar condemned the strike as a violation of Saudi sovereignty and a threat to civilians and aviation safety.
UN envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg warned on Sunday that the attacks threatened regional security and further complicated efforts to secure peace in Yemen.
Airlines extend Riyadh flight cancellations
Riyadh airport remained closed on Monday, with no confirmed time for passenger flights to resume.
A senior aviation source told AFP on Sunday that operators had been informed at dawn that flights would remain suspended. A second aviation source said radar and communications equipment had been damaged and the runways needed to be assessed.
Etihad Airways and Emirates cancelled further Riyadh flights on Monday and Tuesday, The National reported. Flydubai extended its cancellations to Riyadh, Dammam and Abha through Wednesday.
The airport urged passengers to check with their airlines before travelling there.
Lufthansa Group had already suspended flights to Riyadh through Friday following attacks earlier in the week.
SriLankan Airlines suspended its Riyadh flights until 18 October, citing the security incident and ongoing safety assessments.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency widened its warning on Friday to cover more Saudi airspace, citing risks to civilian aircraft from missile and drone attacks, air defence activity and falling debris.
The disruption also affected schools in the Saudi capital. An email sent to parents on Sunday, seen by AFP, said schools would switch to remote learning for the week under instructions from the education ministry.
This was the second time in less than a month that Riyadh schools had been told to move lessons online.

sources.headline: Passenger terminal at Riyadh airport is struck again, a day after 12 were killed
sources.text:
This image from video obtained and verified by AP shows thick black smoke and flames rising from a fire at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (UGC via AP)
AP/UGC
hide caption
AP/UGC
CAIRO — A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others.
Saudi authorities said one person, described as a Pakistani national, was killed, and 11 were injured in the latest attack on the domestic terminal complex at King Khalid International Airport. The airport — struck four times in the past five days — has been closed since Saturday's missile attack, which was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began. Over 300 other people were wounded, some critically. The sharp escalation in the war's new front threatens to draw in greater U.S. military involvement. President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the Houthis. There was no White House comment Sunday.
India's embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died Sunday of injuries sustained in Saturday's attack, which would bring the toll to 13. Saudi authorities later said King Fahd International Airport in Dammam also was attacked, with few details. The city is on the Persian Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar. The latest strike in Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis said the airport in the rebel-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again, and blamed the Saudis. On Sunday night the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel reported further strikes on Sanaa, blaming Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia has not commented on the strikes. At stake, again, in this escalation are global supplies and prices of oil as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz — along with civilians and aviation throughout the region. Trump said he planned to speak to Saudi crown prince There was no sign Sunday that Trump had followed up on plans to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has been seeking assistance against the war-hardened rebel group that is currently Iran's most dynamic proxy. A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen, further restricting the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month. The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces with Yemen's internationally recognized government, has been trying to seize them back.
The rebels' strikes against Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and military facilities highlight a problem. The kingdom is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the Iran war. Some airlines have suspended flights serving Saudi airports, and some embassies have cautioned citizens about the risks of using them, after multiple Houthi warnings about the rebels' use of Saudi airspace. Sunday's attack occurred as the Saudis hosted a major international energy conference in Riyadh, with other high-profile events including an investment gathering on the horizon. Saudi Arabia under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought to open more to the world as a business and tourism destination, but the Houthi attacks threaten those efforts. "There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix, we come out of the ashes all the time," the Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, told the conference. He added that the kingdom is also working on pipelines in addition to the East-West one that was attacked and closed for days last month, with no details.
People gather outside a metro station on the road to King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026.
AP Photo
hide caption
AP Photo
The toll rises on both sides Earlier on Sunday, the Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa. The ministry also said 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks, 60% of them women and children. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims, as fighting in Yemen surges after a major military offensive was launched against the Houthis a week ago. Inside Saudi Arabia, identities emerged for some of those killed in Saturday's attack in Riyadh, including an Egyptian flight attendant and a Syrian widow living in the kingdom.
The government has previously said the dead also include four Saudi citizens, as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, one Palestinian, one American, one Jordanian and one Sudanese national. Early Monday, Saudi Arabia released videos of the moment of the strike captured by security cameras. They show people, many dressed in the white robes of Mecca-bound pilgrims, standing in line in a busy hall, while others scroll phones in a nearby seating area before a fireball erupts, following by people throwing themselves to the floor and running for safety. An expert says the Houthis' tactics could backfire The Houthis until recently had been largely on the Iran war's sidelines. They have developed their military capabilities in recent years to become one of Tehran's most powerful allies. Now they're pressuring its regional rival and a key U.S. ally. Late Sunday, Saudi Arabia and Iran said their foreign ministers had spoken by phone. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he warned against insisting on a military approach and ignoring a political solution, and said Tehran was ready to help start a dialogue between the Saudis and the Houthis. The Saudis and Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war on behalf of the government. Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. The attack revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas. The rebels declared a blockade on Saudi Arabia. Now the Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse Houthi territorial gains. But the rebels' pressure tactics could backfire, said Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group's senior analyst for Yemen: "Rather than pushing Riyadh to step back, attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could make the Saudis more determined to continue the campaign."
Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Collin Binkley in Washington and Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut contributed to this report.

sources.headline: Riyadh airport strike survivors: Houthi missile kills 12, injures 300; residents and travellers recount horror
sources.text: The attack on Saturday killed 12 people and wounded around 300 others, some critically. The airport remained closed on Sunday after another projectile struck a passenger terminal.Passengers and travellers caught up in a deadly missile strike at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport have recounted scenes of panic, bloodshed and confusion, as attacks blamed on Iran-backed Houthi rebels intensified across Saudi Arabia. Survivors described hearing a deafening explosion, seeing severely injured people and scrambling to safety as airport sirens sounded.The attack on Saturday killed 12 people and wounded around 300 others, some critically. The airport remained closed on Sunday after another projectile struck a passenger terminal, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen.'My blood ran cold'A 32-year-old Riyadh resident told that a loud explosion shook the airport before alarm sirens triggered panic among passengers, news agency AFP reported."I heard a very loud noise, so loud that I felt the airport shake," he said, "The airport alarm sirens went off, and that's when the panic started."The man said people from Terminal 3 began running towards them, with several visibly covered in blood. Some had suffered severe injuries, including the loss of a hand or an arm."People who were in Terminal 3 started running towards us. Some had blood covering their faces," he recounted, "Some had lost a hand or an arm. People were running while carrying injured people, covered in blood."The scenes left him terrified and unsure how to respond. "My blood ran cold. I didn't know where to go or what to do," he said.Security personnel escorted him and other passengers to a lower floor. They waited there for about an hour before being allowed to leave the scene.As per the report, the passengers spoke on condition of anonymity because of the harsh measures Saudi authorities have threatened against people who speak publicly about strikes.Doctors describe severe injuries, traumaThe impact of the attack was also felt across Riyadh's hospitals, where the health ministry activated emergency protocols to handle a mass-casualty incident. Doctors were ordered to report to medical facilities across the capital.One doctor told that the number of casualties was unlike anything he had witnessed before. Some religious pilgrims travelling to Mecca arrived at hospitals with their white shrouds stained with blood."The numbers were far higher than anything I had ever seen here before," the doctor said. He described patients with severe limb injuries and shards of glass embedded in their faces and eyes."Patients had severe limb injuries and shards of glass embedded in their faces and eyes," he added, "At least four people suffered severe nervous breakdowns."A Saudi military spokesman described the attack as a "full-fledged war crime".'Talk to us': Residents seek answersBeyond the immediate casualties, repeated attacks and limited information from authorities have fuelled anxiety among residents. Saudi Arabia has remained largely silent about the scale and extent of Houthi attacks over the past three months, leaving people uncertain about the risks ahead.Warning text messages that previously alerted residents to incoming barrages have also fallen silent in recent weeks.According to the report by AFP, one frustrated Riyadh resident the lack of communication was adding to the fear."I want to leave from here," the resident said, "I understand they do not want to cause panic but talk to us. Communication channels will make us feel comfortable."Indian family stranded after flight diversionThe attacks have also disrupted air travel, leaving passengers stranded.An Indian national whose transit flight to Riyadh was diverted to Dammam said he, his wife and their young child had to spend the night at the airport. The family said their airline provided no information and their luggage was lost."We spent the night at the airport -- on the floor and chairs," he said, "Not just us, there were at least one dozen other people around me from the same flight who kept waiting through the night."The experience left him unwilling to transit through the kingdom again."I am never flying through Saudi Arabia again," he said.Another traveller, a 39-year-old woman, said she was aboard a plane heading to Riyadh when it suddenly turned back towards Jeddah. The unexpected change left passengers frightened."We panicked," she said.Asked whether she would fly within Saudi Arabia again while the war continued, she ruled out the possibility."Never. I will never live this horror again," she said.Houthi attacks widens Middle East conflictThe Houthis claimed responsibility for the Saturday strike on Riyadh airport, as well as other strikes on Saudi targets. The Saudi-led coalition said another projectile struck a passenger terminal at King Khalid International Airport on Sunday. There were no immediate details about casualties from the latest strike.The rebels also claimed attacks on King Fahd Airport in Dammam and oil and gas facilities in eastern Saudi Arabia. They warned airlines, airport workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, saying these had become vulnerable to attack. Airports in Mecca and Medina were exempted from the warning.The two sides have been fighting since 2015, when Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in support of the internationally recognised government.The conflict has now raised concerns about the security of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping route at the southern end of the Red Sea. A disruption there could further restrict oil shipments from the Persian Gulf, particularly as the Iran war has already threatened traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.Sunday's strike also came as Riyadh hosted a major international energy conference, with other high-profile gatherings planned.The Saudi-led coalition has been providing air support to Yemeni government forces seeking to reverse recent Houthi gains near Bab el-Mandeb.
